citeAs: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao (2024). MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts. ICLR 2024.
creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao (UCLA, University of Washington, Microsoft Research)
description: MathVista is a benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning of foundation models in visual contexts. It consists of 6,141 examples derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA), covering seven mathematical reasoning types and five primary tasks across diverse visual contexts including natural images, geometry diagrams, charts, and plots.
name: MathVista
publisher: UCLA, University of Washington, Microsoft Research
rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 (three reviewers per item for new datasets and VQA math-labeling; 5 annotators per item for human performance evaluation on testmini)
rai:annotatorDemographics: New dataset annotators: graduate students in STEM fields. Human performance evaluators (AMT): required high school diploma or higher, history of completing more than 5,000 HIT tasks, acceptance score higher than 0.99, must pass qualification questions on elementary math.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-annotator agreement was measured using Fleiss Kappa score (0.775) for mathematical reasoning labeling, indicating substantial consistency. For new dataset annotation, inter-annotation consistency rate was 99.2% (only 6 out of 736 questions had disagreements). For automatic mathematical reasoning category annotation, 94.1% of examples had exact same set of reasoning types between automatic and human annotations, with 98.79% of individual labels identical.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom annotation tool (GUI shown in paper figures); Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) for human performance evaluation
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Three expert annotators manually labeled VQA examples to determine if they involve mathematical reasoning, using majority voting. For the three new datasets, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and refined through a rigorous review process with a two-step annotation: each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, then discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Metadata annotations (question type, answer type, task category, grade level, visual context, reasoning skills) were also applied.
rai:dataBiases: Annotations were sourced from original data providers, resulting in only 85.6% of examples having annotations. Due to the heterogeneity of sources, annotations lack a unified format and structure. The dataset's focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts spanning specific domains like science and college-level math may limit generalizability. Each source dataset was capped at 400 examples to ensure balanced representation.
rai:dataCollection: MathVista was assembled from three sources: (1) nine MathQA datasets in multimodal settings (2,666 examples), (2) 19 general VQA datasets filtered for math-related instances (2,739 examples), and (3) three newly created datasets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA) with 736 newly curated examples. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples to ensure balanced representation.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of 28 existing multimodal datasets (9 MathQA datasets and 19 VQA datasets) plus three newly created datasets. Sources include geometry problem datasets, math word problem datasets, textbook QA datasets, chart/figure QA datasets, and natural image VQA datasets. PaperQA was sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: PaperQA sourced from papers released in August 2023; model evaluations conducted September–October 2023
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: Dataset coverage may have gaps in certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. The focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts spanning specific domains like science and college-level math makes data collection labor-intensive, raising concerns about scalability and generalizability to other domains. Only 85.6% of examples have annotations. Annotations lack unified format due to heterogeneous sources. The study focused exclusively on the most recent and prominent models given rapid development in foundation models.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For VQA datasets, heuristic rules were used to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning: examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words were selected. This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples. Coarse labels of mathematical reasoning were automatically obtained from source dataset details. Each source dataset was limited to up to 400 examples.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The benchmark will be maintained with an online evaluation platform; answer labels for the test set will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination. The authors are committed to maintaining the datasets (e.g., refining potential data noise) in response to community feedback and evolving the leaderboard in response to new models.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MathVista is intended to drive development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks, with applications in educational disciplines, logical queries about statistical data, and theorem proving and scientific discovery in advanced research fields.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs and LMMs in visual contexts; benchmarking foundation models on tasks requiring fine-grained visual understanding and compositional reasoning; facilitating development of mathematical reasoning systems in visually intensive scenarios; model development validation (testmini subset).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: GPT-4 (used as answer extractor with >99.5% accuracy on 200 examples); EasyOCR (used for OCR text detection from images); Multimodal Bard (used for image caption generation to augment LLMs)

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling such as cloud filtering, missing timestamps, or incomplete records in the dataset collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; the dataset does not involve filling in missing values.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation such as augmentation, balancing, or resampling is described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper does not discuss collection of personal or sensitive information; the dataset consists of mathematical reasoning questions with images.
null_reasons.license: License CC-BY-SA-4.0 comes from HuggingFace metadata, not from the paper text. The evidence quote used (about non-English questions) does not support the license claim. The paper itself does not state a license.

evidence.name: we present MATHVISTA, a benchmark designed to combine challenges from diverse mathematical and visual tasks.
evidence.description: It consists of 6,141 examples, derived from 28 existing multimodal datasets involving mathematics and 3 newly created datasets (i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA). Completing these tasks requires fine-grained, deep visual understanding and compositional reasoning, which all state-of-the-art foundation models find challenging.

evidence.isLiveDataset: MATHVISTA consists of 6,141 examples, divided into two subsets: testmini and test. testmini contains 1,000 examples, intended for model development validation or for those with limited computing resources. The testset features the remaining 5,141 examples for standard evaluation.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: We collected nine MathQA datasets in multimodal settings, including four for GPS, two for MWP with visual contexts of synthetic scenes, abstract diagrams, and tables, and two for TQA on college curricula. Each source dataset is limited to up to 400 examples to ensure a balanced representation of each source in our final compiled benchmark. In total, we collected 2,666 examples.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We reviewed more than 70 datasets, collecting 19 of them that contain math-related instances and are publicly available. IQTest comprises 228 examples requiring inductive reasoning, abstract thinking, pattern prediction, and calculations, sourced from puzzle test figures on online learning platforms.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: MATHVISTA incorporates 28 existing multimodal datasets, including 9 math-targeted question answering (MathQA) datasets and 19 VQA datasets. In addition, we have created three new datasets (i.e., IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA) which are tailored to evaluating logical reasoning on puzzle test figures, algebraic reasoning over functional plots, and scientific reasoning with academic paper figures, respectively.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: PaperQA is a novel dataset featuring questions derived from informative academic illustrations, including tables, figures, and charts from online education resources, with 107 examples sourced from papers released in August 2023 on Huggingface.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: we initially designed heuristic rules to automatically select examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning from a large pool of candidates. Examples with numeric answers or those containing quantity words (as listed in §D.1) in the questions were selected. This automatic filtration yielded 4,949 VQA-format examples, though some false positive examples remained.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: To ensure data quality, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and further refined through a rigorous review process. To ensure consistency in annotation, we employed a two-step process. Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Initially, each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers, resulting in a high inter-annotation consistency rate of 99.2%. Specifically, among the newly collected 736 questions, only 6 exhibited disagreements in the annotated answers.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Our analysis yielded a Fleiss Kappa score of 0.775, indicating a substantial level of consistency among the annotators. This high degree of agreement underscores the reliability of our annotation process and affirms the quality of the labeled data generated for our study.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: We developed an annotation tool, as illustrated in Figure 22, to enable expert annotators to label problems that involve mathematical reasoning. Additionally, we established a human performance baseline by engaging qualified human annotators with a high school diploma or higher. We conducted a study to evaluate human performance on the testmini subset of the MATHVISTA, utilizing Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT).
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: To ensure data quality, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and further refined through a rigorous review process. Each question from the testmini subset was assigned to five annotators, all of whom have a history of completing more than 5,000 HIT tasks and boast an acceptance score higher than 0.99, to ensure the quality of the results.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Our benchmark adheres to the following collection guidelines: (1) it covers multiple tasks and topics to mirror real-world applications; (2) it incorporates diverse visual contexts and mathematical skills to foster a well-rounded evaluation; (3) it offers varying levels of challenge to effectively probe and uncover the potential limitations of current models; and (4) it provides robust evaluation settings for deterministic evaluations.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Annotations were sourced from original data providers, resulting in only 85.6% of examples (Table 1) having annotations. Due to the heterogeneity of these sources, annotations lack a unified format and structure. For example, the annotations could be logic forms of the problem parsing from Geometry3K, natural language solutions from TabMWP, and theorems from TheoremQA.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: One limitation is the dataset coverage. While MATHVISTA encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks and visual contexts, there may be gaps in the representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. Furthermore, the dataset's focus on mathematical reasoning within visual contexts, spanning specific domains like science and college-level math, necessitates a more labor-intensive process for collecting high-quality data compared to textual-only or general-purpose datasets. Thus, the scalability and generalizability of our benchmark to other domains remain a concern.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: This significant gap underscores the critical role that MATHVISTA will play in the development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks.
evidence.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: the answer labels for test will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination, and we will maintain an online evaluation platform. Our benchmark is part of an ongoing research process, and we are committed to maintaining the datasets, such as refining the potential data noise, in response to the community feedback. Also, we are committed to evolving the leaderboard in response to new models.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We propose an answer extractor (§F.2) based on LLMs such as GPT-4, inspired by its remarkable ability for text processing. A preliminary study of 200 examples shows that GPT-4 can extract the answer text with more than 99.5% accuracy.
